# Runtimes and Formats: PyTorch, ONNX Runtime and TensorRT

Last verified: 2026-10-28 against PyTorch 2.14 docs (`torch.compile`, `inference_mode`, `torch.onnx`) and the PyTorch source docstrings (TorchScript), the ONNX Runtime execution-provider, TensorRT-EP and CUDA-EP docs and source, and NVIDIA TensorRT docs (engine compatibility, dynamic shapes, precision control, `trtexec`). The compare snippet was run locally.

Scope: general concepts about PyTorch (a Python library for building and running models), ONNX (a file format for models), ONNX Runtime (a program that runs ONNX files) and TensorRT (NVIDIA's tool that compiles a model for one kind of GPU) as public tools. This lesson says nothing about how any particular company's serving stack is built. In week 1, replace the generic nouns below with the real ones.

Builds on: the request stages and GPU kernels (lessons inference-runtimes/01-serving-anatomy, gpu-fundamentals/01-gpu-architecture-and-roofline); Kubernetes pods and nodes (lesson containers-ci/03-kubernetes-for-a-service-engineer).

## The problem and why it matters

The same trained model can be executed by several different engines. Each makes a different trade between flexibility, speed, portability and risk. A senior engineer is asked: "should we convert this model?", "why did the new build crash on the new GPUs?", "why do outputs differ slightly after export?".

You need to know what each runtime is, what a converted artifact is tied to, and how to prove the conversion did not change the answers.

## First principles

1. **A model is weights plus a computation graph** (the operations, such as matrix multiplies, and how data flows between them). A runtime is whatever executes that graph on hardware.
2. **Eager execution runs one operation at a time from Python.** It is flexible and easy to debug, and each operation pays launch overhead. A compiler that sees the whole graph can fuse operations (merge several into one GPU program) and pick better kernels.
3. **An interchange format separates producer from consumer.** ONNX describes a graph in a framework-neutral way. Anything the consumer's operator set (the list of operations it supports) lacks cannot be exported or run.
4. **An engine is a compiled artifact (a build output file) tied to its build environment.** TensorRT's docs say, by default, engines are compatible only with the TensorRT version that built them and only with the type of device where they were built.
5. **Lower precision trades accuracy for speed and memory.** FP16 and INT8 (16-bit float and 8-bit integer numbers, versus the usual 32-bit float) shrink and speed things up, and they change the numbers. INT8 stores values with a scaling factor; NVIDIA's docs name two workflows for getting it, post-training quantization and quantization-aware training.
6. **Every conversion is a code change.** Treat it like one: pin versions, diff the outputs, keep the old path to roll back to.

## How it works

### The path from training to serving

```
 PyTorch model (eager)
    │
    ├──▶ serve directly (+ torch.compile)
    │
    ├──▶ export ──▶ ONNX file (portable graph)
    │                  │
    │                  ├──▶ ONNX Runtime
    │                  │      providers: TensorRT,
    │                  │      CUDA, CPU
    │                  │
    │                  └──▶ TensorRT builder
    │                          │
    │                          ▼
    │                     engine / plan
    │                  (this GPU + this TRT)
    ▼
 each arrow: validate outputs against eager
```

TRT is short for TensorRT, and a plan is TensorRT's saved engine file. Moving right trades flexibility for speed and hardware tie-in. The ONNX file is the portable middle; the engine is the least portable end.

### PyTorch: eager, compile, inference mode

Eager is the default. For serving, wrap forward passes in `torch.inference_mode()` (it turns off the bookkeeping PyTorch keeps for training; autograd is its gradient-recording system, and a tensor is a multi-dimensional array of numbers): the docs say that compared with `no_grad` it removes additional overhead by disabling view tracking and version-counter bumps, and that tensors created in it cannot be used in computations recorded by autograd.

`torch.compile` captures graphs with TorchDynamo (which records your Python code as a graph) and by default compiles with the TorchInductor backend (which turns that graph into fast GPU code). Its documented modes: `"default"`, `"reduce-overhead"` (uses CUDA graphs, a recorded sequence of GPU work replayed with one launch, to cut Python overhead, useful for small batches), `"max-autotune"`, and `"max-autotune-no-cudagraphs"`. With `dynamic=None` it detects dynamism and recompiles with a more dynamic kernel; `dynamic=False` always specialises; `fullgraph=True` requires the whole function to be one graph rather than silently falling back. Operationally: the first call per new shape is slow, so warm up the shapes you expect, and watch for recompilation in production. TorchScript is an older capture path. The PyTorch source marks its helper functions "deprecated since 2.5" and says "please use `torch.compile` instead", so do not build anything new on it.

### ONNX and execution providers

ONNX Runtime (ORT) uses *execution providers* (EPs). A model is a graph of operations (each one a *node*, such as a matrix multiply). ORT splits that graph into groups of nodes and hands each group to the first EP in your priority list that supports it, on that EP's hardware. Nodes no listed EP can take fall back to the CPU.

```
 providers = [TensorRT, CUDA, CPU]

   graph:  A ─ B ─ C ─ D ─ E ─ F
           └──TRT──┘   │   └CUDA┘
                       └ no TRT/CUDA kernel:
                         falls to CPU
   cost: each provider boundary can mean
         a copy and a sync point
```

A sync point is where the CPU waits for the GPU to catch up. The risk: a model that "runs on GPU" but has a few nodes silently on CPU, with copies between. Measure rather than assume: compare against a CPU-only run, and print the registered providers (below). How ORT reports per-node placement was not checked here.

```python
import onnxruntime as ort

providers = [
    ("TensorrtExecutionProvider", {"trt_fp16_enable": True,
                                   "trt_engine_cache_enable": True,
                                   "trt_engine_cache_path": "/var/cache/trt"}),
    "CUDAExecutionProvider",
    "CPUExecutionProvider",
]
sess = ort.InferenceSession("model.onnx", providers=providers)
print(sess.get_providers())     # what was actually registered
```

Option names above are from the ORT docs. Not run here (no ORT or GPU on this Mac). Always print the providers that registered: if CUDA fails to load you may end up on CPU with only a log warning. In ORT's Python binding source, a provider that fails to create logs "Failed to create ..." and is skipped, with no exception (an unknown provider name does raise). Docs do not describe this, and it may differ by version.

Exporting from PyTorch uses `torch.onnx.export`. Per the PyTorch docs the torch.export-based exporter (`dynamo=True`) is now the default, `opset_version=None` picks the recommended opset (version of ONNX's operation list), and `dynamic_shapes` is the preferred way to mark variable dimensions (`dynamic_axes` is deprecated for that exporter). Not run here.

### TensorRT: build once, run on matching hardware

```
 BUILD (slow, once)               RUN (fast, many)
 ┌──────────────────┐            ┌─────────────────┐
 │ ONNX + profile   │            │ load .plan      │
 │ + precision      │ ─────────▶ │ same GPU type,  │
 │ tries kernels on │  engine    │ same TRT version│
 │ this GPU         │  file      │ shapes in range │
 └──────────────────┘            └─────────────────┘
```

Key facts, from NVIDIA's docs:
- The builder auto-tunes (tries many kernel variants and keeps the fastest) against an **optimisation profile** with min, opt and max shapes per dynamic input. Memory use can change a lot with those values, and some tactics (candidate kernel strategies) only work when min = opt = max.
- Engines are by default only compatible with the TensorRT version that built them and the device type where they were built. The plan records version and compute capability (NVIDIA's version number for a GPU's hardware generation) and fails to deserialise (load back into memory) on mismatch.
- Relaxations exist and cost performance: hardware-compatibility levels (`kAMPERE_PLUS`, `kSAME_COMPUTE_CAPABILITY`) can lower throughput or raise latency; `VERSION_COMPATIBLE` plans can be slower and contain executable code, so deserialise only trusted ones.
- ONNX Runtime's TensorRT EP says engine and profile files "are not portable", and says to clean up old cache files when the model, ORT version or TensorRT version changes (hardware changes are in its environment-variables section). Its first run (warmup) "can be very long" because building the engine involves exhaustive profiling, so enable the engine cache and warm it ahead of traffic. It also says that if input shapes are out of range of the cached engine's profile, the profile cache is updated and the engine is recreated, which is a stall on the request that triggers it. NVIDIA's TensorRT pages say nothing about out-of-range shapes.

A command-line build, using flags from NVIDIA's `trtexec` docs (`trtexec` is TensorRT's command-line build and benchmark tool) (not run here; shape syntax is `name:AxBxC`):

```bash
trtexec --onnx=model.onnx --saveEngine=model.plan \
  --minShapes=input:1x3x224x224 \
  --optShapes=input:8x3x224x224 \
  --maxShapes=input:32x3x224x224
```

Precision: NVIDIA's `latest` docs say that since TensorRT 11.0 only strongly typed networks are supported, meaning the model specifies the precision of every tensor, and the `trtexec` README says builder precision flags such as `--int8` or `--best` cannot be combined with `--stronglyTyped`. `--fp16` appears only in README examples (DLA), not in the flag list I read. So on TensorRT 11 expect precision to come from the model, and on older versions or via ORT use `trt_fp16_enable` ("enable FP16 mode in TensorRT"); check `trtexec --help` on your version.

### Validate after converting

```python
import numpy as np

def compare(ref, test, rtol=1e-3, atol=1e-4):
    diff = np.abs(ref.astype(np.float64) - test.astype(np.float64))
    return {"max_abs": float(diff.max()),
            "mean_abs": float(diff.mean()),
            "allclose": bool(np.allclose(ref, test, rtol=rtol, atol=atol)),
            "top1_agree": float((ref.argmax(-1) == test.argmax(-1)).mean())}
```

This comparison was run locally on synthetic data with a simulated FP16 round-trip. The tolerances shown (rtol and atol: how far two numbers may differ, relatively and absolutely, and still count as equal) are placeholders: choose them from how much error your task can tolerate. Compare on real, varied inputs, including the longest and shortest and edge cases, and compare a task metric (accuracy, WER which is word error rate for speech, whatever you ship) and not only raw tensors. Small tensor differences can be fine; a metric drop is not.

## Worked failure scenario

**Symptom:** a new node pool (a group of identical machines in a Kubernetes cluster) joins. Pods (Kubernetes' running copies of your server) on it crash-loop (start, fail and restart repeatedly) at startup. Pods on the old pool are fine. The same image and the same model files.

1. **Read the first error line.** A deserialisation or "incompatible" error from the runtime points at the engine file, not the app.
2. **Compare environments.** GPU model and compute capability, TensorRT or ORT version, driver version, between a good pod and a bad pod.
3. **Where did the engine come from?** If it was built on the old GPU type and baked into the image or shared volume, the docs say it is by default only valid on the device type that built it.
4. **Is the cache path shared?** Two GPU types writing to one cache directory can serve each other wrong files. Key the cache by GPU type and TensorRT version.
5. **If the load works but outputs look off:** run `compare` between eager and the engine on a fixed input set. Check precision settings, INT8 scaling factors, and shapes outside the profile.

**Fix:** ship the portable ONNX file and build (or fetch from a cache keyed by GPU type and TRT version) the engine at deploy or startup, then warm it before marking ready. Pin and record: model hash, opset, exporter version, TRT/ORT version, GPU arch, driver. Keep the previous runtime path switchable so you can roll back without rebuilding.

## Tradeoffs

| Use when | Avoid when |
|---|---|
| Eager or `torch.compile`: model changes often, custom Python logic, fast iteration | Latency budget needs more than the framework can give and you can validate a conversion |
| ONNX Runtime: need portability across hardware, or a non-Python host | Model uses ops the opset or EPs lack, forcing CPU fallback |
| TensorRT: stable model, fixed GPU fleet, tight latency or cost | Frequent model changes, mixed GPU types you cannot build for, no way to validate numerics |
| FP16 or INT8: memory or speed is the constraint and metrics survive | The task is precision-sensitive and you have no regression set |

First profile. If time is spent in preprocessing, queueing or copies, converting the model will not help.

## Interview questions

1. What is ONNX and what does ONNX Runtime add? *Probe:* what is an execution provider? *Outline:* neutral graph format; runtime that partitions the graph across EPs in priority order with CPU fallback.
2. Why is a TensorRT engine not portable? *Probe:* what changes require a rebuild? *Outline:* tuned to GPU and TRT version; rebuild on new GPU type, TRT upgrade, model, precision or profile change.
3. What are min/opt/max shapes? *Probe:* what if production traffic sits far from opt? *Outline:* the range the auto-tuner optimises over, and the shape it favours; include real sizes; in ORT's TensorRT EP a shape outside the cached profile triggers an engine rebuild, and NVIDIA's docs do not say what plain TensorRT does.
4. How do you prove a converted model is correct? *Outline:* fixed inputs, tensor diffs with tolerances, task metrics on a held-out set, edge cases, compare per precision.
5. When would you not convert? *Outline:* model churn, unsupported ops, bottleneck elsewhere, no validation capacity.
6. How do you version and roll back converted artifacts? *Outline:* record every input of the build; key caches by hardware and version; keep the old path live.
7. A model "runs on GPU" in ORT but is slow. Why? *Outline:* nodes fell back to CPU, copies between providers, CUDA EP failed to load.

**Worked exercise:** draw the path from PyTorch to a TensorRT engine for an image model with a variable batch size. Mark which artifacts are portable, which keys the engine cache needs, and the three checks you run before sending traffic.

## Checklist

1. I can say what eager, `torch.compile`, ONNX and TensorRT each are and give one reason to pick each.
2. I can explain execution providers and CPU fallback.
3. I can explain why an engine is tied to GPU and TensorRT version.
4. I can write down a conversion validation plan with tolerances and a task metric.
5. I can list what to record to reproduce and roll back an artifact.

## Common wrong answers

- "Convert to TensorRT, it is always faster." Only if the model is the bottleneck, and you re-validated.
- "The engine file is just the model." It is a build product for one environment.
- "Outputs differ slightly, so it's broken." Maybe not; compare with tolerances and a task metric.
- "ONNX Runtime on GPU means everything runs on GPU." Unsupported nodes fall back.

## Sources

Consulted and checked:
- torch.compile API (https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.compile.html): default backend "inductor", `mode` values, `dynamic` None/True/False, `fullgraph`.
- torch.compiler overview (https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/user_guide/torch_compiler/torch.compiler.html): Dynamo, Inductor.
- `inference_mode` (https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.autograd.grad_mode.inference_mode.html): disables view tracking and version counter bumps; tensors cannot be used in autograd-recorded computations. The page does not say "faster than no_grad", so the lesson no longer does.
- TorchScript status: docstrings in https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pytorch/pytorch/main/torch/jit/__init__.py ("deprecated:: 2.5", "TorchScript is deprecated, please use torch.compile instead"). The 2.14 `jit.html` page rendered empty here, so the source was used.
- torch.onnx (https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/onnx.html): `dynamo=True` default since 2.9, `opset_version=None` uses the recommended version, `dynamic_axes` deprecated in favour of `dynamic_shapes`.
- ONNX Runtime EPs (https://onnxruntime.ai/docs/execution-providers/): priority order, `get_providers`. TensorRT EP (https://onnxruntime.ai/docs/execution-providers/TensorRT-ExecutionProvider.html): option names and descriptions, non-portable engines, cache-invalidation list, long first run, rebuild on out-of-range shapes, fallback of unsupported subgraphs to CUDA or CPU.
- ORT Python binding source (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/microsoft/onnxruntime/main/onnxruntime/python/onnxruntime_pybind_state.cc): a failed provider creation logs a warning and the provider is skipped; first 200k characters read.
- TensorRT engine compatibility (https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/tensorrt/latest/inference-library/engine-compatibility.html): version and device-type defaults, `kAMPERE_PLUS`, `kSAME_COMPUTE_CAPABILITY`, `VERSION_COMPATIBLE`, failure to deserialise on mismatch.
- TensorRT dynamic shapes (.../dynamic-shapes-basics.html): min/opt/max feed the auto-tuner, memory "can change dramatically", some tactics need MIN=OPT=MAX. Precision control (.../precision-control.html): "Since 11.0, TensorRT supports only Strongly Typed networks." Quantized types (.../work-quantized-types.html): INT8 uses a scaling factor; PTQ and QAT workflows.
- trtexec: flags `--onnx`, `--saveEngine`, `--minShapes/--optShapes/--maxShapes`, `name:AxBxC` syntax (https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/tensorrt/latest/performance/benchmarking.html, first 100k of 115k characters); `--stronglyTyped` incompatibility with `--int8`/`--best` (https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT/blob/main/samples/trtexec/README.md). `--fp16` is documented in neither as a flag description. Not run here (no TensorRT, no GPU).
- The `compare` snippet was run locally on synthetic data. The ORT and `torch.onnx` snippets were not run here (no ORT or GPU on this Mac).

Not checked: how ORT reports per-node placement, what plain TensorRT does for shapes outside the profile, the INT8 calibration procedure.
